title: Baltic spy chiefs warn Moscow is preparing for more decisive action in Europe
summary:
Exclusive: intelligence officers warn campaign against Nato could intensify ‘in months, not years’ – but panic will play into Kremlin psy-ops

European intelligence officials have raised the…
byline: Shaun Walker in Prague and Riga

blocks.text: European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months not years”.

The warnings came after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggest Russia may launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”.

French president Emmanuel Macron called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented”, and on Friday summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting in Paris, where they discussed – among other topics – intelligence of a growing threat from Russia.

The escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine. Kyiv hit Moscow and other Russian regions with hundreds of drones and missiles in the early hours of Sunday, in one of its biggest air attacks of the war.

blocks.caption: Russian president Vladimir Putin, pictured here alongside Adm Viktor Liina, commander of Russia’s Pacific fleet. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In separate interviews with the Guardian over the past week, in different locations, three European intelligence leaders discussed their views of the potential threat from Moscow.

Michal Koudelka, head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service, said that as well as increased drone activity, a small-scale invasion of Nato territory that borders Russia could be part of the Kremlin’s plans. “It’s possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said, in a rare interview at the agency’s headquarters in Prague. He said this scenario could play out in a matter of “months, not years,” but added that “a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn’t happen”.

Officials in the three Baltic nations, which border Russian territory, have been more cautious about the prospect of an invasion or other serious escalation, citing Moscow’s currently stretched resources in Ukraine and warning that playing up the prospect of a massive attack might be to play into the Kremlin’s hands.

“We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” said Normunds Mežviets, director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service, in an interview at the agency’s headquarters in Riga. He conceded that there are signs that Moscow is making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans are simply part of a destabilisation strategy.
“It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said.

blocks.caption: Michal Koudelka, director of the Czech Republic’s Security Information Service (BIS). Photograph: CTK/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

blocks.text: Baltic politicians, who for many years criticised western Europe for being soft on Russia, now find themselves in the strange position of telling some western leaders to calm down in their public messaging, fearing that talk of an imminent invasion could prove damaging to their societies and economies.

On Saturday, the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, decried “panic on social media” in recent days about a possible attack. “If there is reason to fear an attack, rest assured: we will make that clear. Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine,” he wrote on X.

Mežviets said that, overall, it was good thing that western Europe had woken up to the threat from Russia. “Before 2022, we constantly warned our western European partners about the threat from Russia, but most of the time our voices were not listened to. In 2022, the approach of our partners changed, they said it turns out the Balts and the Poles had been right,” he said.

Neither Mežviets nor Koudelka would discuss what specific intelligence may have been obtained about Russia’s supposed planning for the coming months, nor would they comment on whether a surprise trip by CIA director John Ratcliffe to Moscow last month – during which he stopped off in Riga – was partly to warn the Kremlin about the dangers of launching an attack on Nato.

After that visit, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed rumours of a Russian attack on Nato: “It has nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation,” he said.

blocks.caption: CIA director John Ratcliffe, who made a surprise trip to Moscow last month. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

blocks.text: However, many in Europe will have the build up to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in the back of their minds, when US officials repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invade and the Kremlin repeatedly denied it.

As the full-scale war that ensued approaches its fifth winter, US-led efforts to bring about peace in Ukraine show no signs of success, with both Russia and Ukraine intensifying their drone and missile strikes on each other. Ukraine has destroyed much of Russia’s oil infrastructure, targeting refineries and other facilities over recent months.

Moscow has frequently said that the provision to Ukraine of weaponry, intelligence and military advisers makes western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets, but has so far avoided action that might provoke a coordinated response from Nato. Instead, it has launched what western agencies describe as a campaign of sabotage against targets in countries that are the loudest backers of Ukraine, and one-off incidents apparently meant to test boundaries, such as when more than a dozen drones, flying without ammunition, veered into Polish airspace a year ago.

Koudelka said the current Russian tactic was “escalate to de-escalate”, with the Kremlin keen to push at weak points in western societies to tamp down their support for Ukraine’s war effort. “They believe if they escalate enough then European countries will decide not to support Ukraine,” he said.

blocks.caption: A Russian Shahed drone on display in Kyiv. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP

blocks.text: The escalation fears come as the Trump administration makes another attempt to kickstart peace negotiations in Ukraine. As well as the Ratcliffe visit to Moscow, White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also made another trip to Moscow in recent weeks, as well as a first-time trip to Kyiv. While Donald Trump has frequently claimed Russian president Vladimir Putin is interested in a deal, there is scepticism in Europe that the Kremlin has any interest in good-faith negotiations.

“I haven’t seen any signs that there is a serious consideration in Moscow about real negotiations,” said Thomas Nilsson, head of Sweden’s military intelligence and security service, in an interview on the sidelines of a conference in Riga. “My assessment is that they are still thinking that they could achieve their strategic objectives, so they are just playing negotiation theatre,” he added.

All three intelligence bosses said that whatever else happens, Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe is likely to intensify in the coming months. Nilsson described as a “gamechanger” the recent armed drone incident at Leipzig airport, which German authorities have attributed to Russian intelligence.

“To have an armed UAV drone sent in to a busy airport in the middle of Europe … If you have attacks that could result in losses of life or losses of very critical infrastructure that have a huge implication for society, I think that is a gamechanger,” he said.

blocks.caption: A Ukrainian soldier engages an incoming jet-powered Shahed drone during a Russian aerial attack on Kyiv in August. Photograph: Libkos/Getty Images

blocks.text: Mežviets said Russia was moving from randomised targeting of sabotage and arson attacks intended to sow panic to specific targets linked to western backing for Ukraine. “We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure. Right now we see a move towards defence industry targets,” he said. “If you do this then the psy-op effect is reached anyway, so you get both things in one,” he added.

Nilsson said there were several goals behind the recent intensification of Russian sabotage activity: to reduce support for Ukraine, to introduce splits in Nato and to alarm European populations. “I think Moscow would love Nato to have endless discussion about Article 4 consultations, but coming up with no actions,” he said.

Koudelka said another effect of the sabotage campaign is the stretch on resources of intelligence services, as doubts often linger even when incidents are caused by other factors. “Now, every fire or every malfunction needs to be investigated by intelligence services as a potential terror attack, and that is a good result for them,” he said.
